nameStory: The Bay Nettle gets its name from its preferred habitat in coastal bays and estuaries, where it's especially abundant in places like the Chesapeake Bay. The 'nettle' part refers to its stinging cells, which deliver a burning sensation similar to being brushed by stinging nettle plants on land.
description: The Bay Nettle is a translucent, bell-shaped jellyfish that drifts through the brackish and saltwater bays of New England's coast. Its gelatinous body pulses rhythmically as it moves through the water, trailing long, thread-like tentacles behind it. These jellies are typically a few inches across their bell, though they can grow larger in ideal conditions. Like all sea nettles, they pack a painful sting that can leave swimmers with welts and burning sensations.

idTips.label: Bell Shape
idTips.description: Translucent, dome-shaped bell that's squishy and gelatinous to touch, pulsing rhythmically as it swims

idTips.label: Trailing Tentacles
idTips.description: Long, thin tentacles that stream behind the bell like invisible fishing line - nearly transparent and easy to miss

idTips.label: Stinging Sensation
idTips.description: Contact causes immediate burning, stinging pain similar to a bee sting, followed by red welts on skin

idTips.label: Swimming Motion
idTips.description: Moves with a distinctive pulsing contraction of its bell, followed by a graceful drift

idTips.label: Transparency
idTips.description: Nearly see-through body with a slightly milky or opalescent quality, making it hard to spot in water

habitat: Bay Nettles prefer the brackish waters where rivers meet the sea, thriving in New England's coastal estuaries, bays, and harbors. They're commonly found in areas with moderate salinity levels and are often spotted near docks, in shallow coves, and around salt marshes. These jellies favor warmer water temperatures and calm conditions.

seasonality.spring: Bay Nettles begin appearing in warmer coastal waters as temperatures rise, though they're still relatively uncommon in early spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for Bay Nettles - they're most abundant and visible during hot summer months when water temperatures are highest and swimming encounters are most likely.
seasonality.fall: Numbers begin to decline as water temperatures cool, though some individuals may persist into early fall in protected bays.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters during cold winter months, unable to survive the frigid temperatures.

funFact: The Bay Nettle was hiding in plain sight for decades - scientists only realized in 2017 that it was actually a completely separate species from its close cousin, the Atlantic Sea Nettle, despite both being studied extensively for years!
confusionNotes: Bay Nettles are easily confused with Atlantic Sea Nettles, as they're nearly identical in appearance and were considered the same species until recently. The main difference is habitat preference - Bay Nettles favor lower-salinity estuarine waters while Atlantic Sea Nettles prefer full ocean salinity. When in doubt, note the location: if you're in a bay or estuary, it's likely a Bay Nettle.
contextualKnowledge: Until 2017, what we now call Bay Nettles were lumped together with Atlantic Sea Nettles under the scientific name Chrysaora quinquecirrha. This recent species split means many older field guides and references won't distinguish between the two, so don't be surprised if you find conflicting information in different sources.
compareHints: Bay Nettles are virtually identical in appearance to Atlantic Sea Nettles, but they prefer different salinity levels - Bay Nettles thrive in the brackish water of estuaries while Atlantic Sea Nettles prefer full ocean salinity. Both deliver painful stings and have the same translucent, pulsing bell shape with trailing tentacles. The easiest way to tell them apart is simply noting where you found them - estuarine waters usually mean Bay Nettle.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its closest relative the Bay Nettle, the Atlantic Sea Nettle prefers full marine saltwater rather than the brackish estuarine waters favored by Bay Nettles.
